sense.text:
Christ said it: “And then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another.” That is the ground of this whole class, from brother to betrayer. Brothers turning into betrayers is nothing new. Christ foretold it, and it has happened among our people before, in the days of the Maccabees, when a high priest was betrayed by his friend, by his own blood brother, and by men of his own nation.

So the way to understand what Christ said is to go back into the history and see how brothers became betrayers, and then examine ourselves, because the same spirits are among us today.

precepts.why:
“For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.” After reading what Christ said, we go back historically to the brothers who became betrayers, because those histories were written for our learning.

The same verse was read again at the close of the class: what was read in Maccabees pertains to us even today, because there are men and women among us with those same hateful attributes. The history of Simon, Jason and Menelaus is written so that we can see ourselves in it and examine ourselves.

sense.text: Judas Maccabeus armed every one of his men “not so much with defence of shields and spears, as with comfortable and good words”, and told them “a dream worthy to be believed”. That dream inspired them to keep fighting.

This shows the character of Onias, a brother and a priest: Onias III, the high priest in the days of the Maccabees. He was “a virtuous and a good man, reverend in conversation, gentle in condition, well spoken also, and exercised from a child in all points of virtue”, and he “prayed for the whole body of the Jews.” This is the good brother the whole history turns on, the man who was betrayed.

The dream had both Onias and Jeremiah in it. Onias said of Jeremiah, “This is a lover of the brethren, who prayeth much for the people, and for the holy city”, and Jeremiah gave Judas “a sword of gold”, saying, “Take this holy sword, a gift from God, with the which thou shalt wound the adversaries.”

Those words stirred the young men “to valour”, and they set courageously upon the enemy “because the city and the sanctuary and the temple were in danger.”

“The care that they took for their wives, and their children, their brethren, and kinsfolks, was in least account with them: but the greatest and principal fear was for the holy temple.” It is not that they did not care for their wives, their children and their brethren. Their love for the temple was greater than the love of brother and sister, man and wife.

Jerusalem was “inhabited with all peace, and the laws were kept very well, because of the godliness of Onias the high priest, and his hatred of wickedness”. This is the same Onias read about at the beginning.

A man’s faith helps other people’s faith. Because of Onias’s faith, his strength and his love for God’s laws, everybody else was inspired, and the laws were kept very well. And his hatred of wickedness is the mentality we all must have.

Even the kings honoured the place and gave the temple their best gifts because of this man: “Seleucus of Asia of his own revenues bare all the costs belonging to the service of the sacrifices.”

Alexander had four generals: Lysimachus over Thrace and Asia Minor, Cassander over Macedonia and Greece, Ptolemy over Egypt, and Seleucus over Babylon and Syria. This king came out of Seleucus’s line.

“But one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city.” Highlight this man’s name and his tribe.

The governor of the temple managed the temple’s resources, making sure the offerings and donations were accounted for and used for their intended purposes; he saw to the upkeep of the temple, helped order the worship and the scheduling of the sacrifices, handled disputes among the priests and worshippers, worked alongside the high priest, and kept the temple grounds secure. But the high priest was over him regarding the temple. Onias and Simon were working together over the temple, and they had a falling out.

“And when he could not overcome Onias”: whatever Onias said as high priest, it stood, and Simon did not agree with it. So what did he do? He “gat him to Apollonius the son of Thraseas, who then was governor of Celosyria and Phenice”. He ran to the other nations against his own high priest. You can’t make this stuff up.

Jerusalem is down in Palestine; Celosyria is up by Damascus. That is where Simon of the tribe of Benjamin went, to deal with the other nations dwelling there.

He was so mad at Onias that he went and told the other nations “that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money, so that the multitude of their riches, which did not pertain to the account of the sacrifices, was innumerable, and that it was possible to bring all into the king’s hand.” You don’t want to do what I say? I’m going to tell the other nations about all the money in the temple.

The riches that did not pertain to the sacrifices were the tithes: the first tithe for the Levites, because the Levites had no inheritance in the land and served full time in the temple; a tithe of that tithe for the priests; and every third year a store laid up to feed the Levites, the widows, the orphans and the strangers. Those strangers were first and foremost Israelites of another tribe, a man of Judah or of Issachar who was travelling. In certain times money was also set aside to repair and maintain the temple. That is the money Simon told the nations about.

precepts.why:
“Ye that love the Lord, hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked.” Onias hated wickedness, and that is the mentality we all must have. For the Lord to deliver us out of the hand of the wicked, we must begin to train ourselves to hate evil.

A lot of you say you hate evil, but as long as you watch pornography, you don’t hate evil. As long as you watch the black woman twerking up and down, you don’t hate evil. You might go on the street and say you hate evil, but at home you don’t hate evil.

“I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.”

The work of them that turn aside is the brothers and sisters who leave from the truth. When they leave they always say, we’re still serving God, we keep the commandments, I’ve been in ministry thirty-five years. But see them a year or two from now and they are not serving the Lord. They’re back with Easter, back with Thanksgiving, back beating piñatas. God hates the work of them that turn aside, and it must not cleave to us.

Christ said: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” You put your hand to the plough to do the work. Then you get so frustrated with brothers always correcting you, because you’re doing stupid stuff, that you separate yourself to do your own thing.

When you turn back, regardless of your great speech about still keeping the commandments, you have taken your hand off the plough and looked back, and Christ said you are not fit for the kingdom of God. You can try to manipulate his words all you want to justify it.

“Every friend saith, I am his friend also: but there is a friend, which is only a friend in name. Is it not a grief unto death, when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy? O wicked imagination, whence camest thou in to cover the earth with deceit? There is a companion, which rejoiceth in the prosperity of a friend, but in the time of trouble will be against him.”

That is Simon. He and Onias had a dispute, and because of that argument he ran to the other nations and told them about all the money in Jerusalem. A friend only in name, a companion turned to an enemy: a no good dude.

This is what the money in the temple was for: “At the end of three years thou shalt bring forth all the tithe of thine increase the same year, and shalt lay it up within thy gates: And the Levite, (because he hath no part nor inheritance with thee,) and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, which are within thy gates, shall come, and shall eat and be satisfied; that the Lord thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hand which thou doest.”

The scriptures tell you the monies collected were for the Levites, the strangers, the fatherless and the widows. That is what Simon told the nations to come and take.

Tobit says, “I did many almsdeeds to my brethren”. He was of the northern kingdom, carried into the Assyrian captivity at Nineve. “All the tribe of Nephthali my father fell from the house of Jerusalem”: they went against God’s laws, and “sacrificed unto the heifer Baal.”

“But I alone went often to Jerusalem at the feasts, as it was ordained unto all the people of Israel by an everlasting decree, having the firstfruits and tenths of increase”. “The first tenth part of all increase I gave to the sons of Aaron, who ministered at Jerusalem: another tenth part I sold away, and went, and spent it every year at Jerusalem: And the third I gave unto them to whom it was meet, as Debora my father’s mother had commanded me, because I was left an orphan by my father.”

That is the tithe that was laid up in the temple: the priests were provided for, and the third went to them it was meet for, the orphans. Tobit was an orphan himself.

“Behold, we are yet this day in our captivity, where thou hast scattered us, for a reproach and a curse, and to be subject to payments, according to all the iniquities of our fathers, which departed from the Lord our God.”

Brothers often get this wrong. We always harp on “subject to payments”, but when asked why we are subject to payments we give a general answer: sin. No, it tells you why: “according to all the iniquities of our fathers”. What were our fathers supposed to be paying for that we stopped paying for? The Levites, the widows, the strangers, the orphans. We stopped doing that, so now we are in a foreign land subject to payments.

You’re mad about child support. Had we been taking care of the orphans, the widows, the fatherless and the Levites, we would not be subject to payments. Because of this, every month we’ve got a bunch of payments to pay.

“Offend not against the multitude of a city, and then thou shalt not cast thyself down among the people.” What Simon of the tribe of Benjamin did was an offence to the city. He ran to the other nations and told them there was money there for them to take, money meant for the widows, the orphans, the strangers and the Levites. He knew what it was for, but he wanted it used for something else.

“Bind not one sin upon another; for in one thou shalt not be unpunished.” It is never just one sin. Sin works like dominoes: one hits the next and it goes all around. You might think you did just one sin, but examine it and you will see the multitude of sins we often do.

“Say not, God will look upon the multitude of my oblations, and when I offer to the most high God, he will accept it.” You think you can purposely do evil and God will forgive you anyway. Simon would rather help the Greeks up in Celosyria than his own people.

sense.text: Simon told this Edomite, Apollonius, and Apollonius went to the king. The king sent “Heliodorus his treasurer” with “a commandment to bring him the foresaid money.” Bring me all that money.

Heliodorus went “under a colour of visiting the cities of Celosyria and Phenice, but indeed to fulfil the king’s purpose.” That is what he let everybody think he was doing; it was really to take all the money from Jerusalem.

He was “courteously received of the high priest”, told him what he had heard, “and asked if these things were so indeed.” Do you have money laid up for the widows, the orphans, the fatherless, the strangers and the Levites?

“Then the high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children”. The high priest is Onias III, and he says yes, there is money for the widows and the fatherless. The temple had money in it for them.

The temple had money laid up for widows, so why were the widows here “neglected in the daily ministration”? Why didn’t they just get it from the temple? Because these were followers of Christ, and the priesthood had already agreed to cast out anyone who confessed him. Peter and them saw that the widows were not getting anything from the temple because they believed in Christ.
“It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.” To serve tables means to take care of the widows, the orphans and all of that.
“Look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.” This is how the deacons were chosen.
“But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.”

They chose “Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost”. Stephen, the one we always read about, was one of the first deacons chosen. They set the seven before the apostles, “and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.”

precepts.why:
“For the Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.” They were kicking people out left and right.

So in Acts 6 the widows who believed in Christ were getting nothing from the temple, and the apostles had to see to them themselves. That is why the murmuring arose and why the deacons were chosen.

How did they choose seven men of honest report? “Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre; Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.”

“Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.” They did not just look at the man; they looked at his wife too. Sometimes you find a brother who appears decent, but his wife is ratchet, low down, no damn good. That is a reflection on you, brother: if your wife is low down, you ain’t guiding her right.

“Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.” That is how they gauged the men: they looked at the man, then at the wife, and said, he has wisdom, he is of honest report, and they chose seven.

sense.text: What is a widow? You may say a sister whose husband died. But “Honour widows that are widows indeed.” She has to be a widow indeed, and Paul breaks down what that means.
If a widow has children or nephews, they are to “shew piety at home, and to requite their parents”. Her own family comes first.

“Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.” A widow had a duty. She trusted in God and continued in supplications and prayers night and day.

“But she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth.” The widows made a kind of vow to dedicate themselves to the Lord and pray night and day for the benefit of Israel. She that lives in pleasure has reneged on that.

“But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.” If a widow has family, her family is to look after her first and foremost: her kin, her relatives.

“Let not a widow be taken into the number”: there was a widowhood of sisters whose job was to pray for Israel, fasting and praying night and day. She did not just sit around saying, my husband died, I’m a widow. She had a duty, an obligation.

To be taken into the number she had to be a widow indeed, not “under threescore years old”, and “the wife of one man”, married to only one man in her life. She had to be “well reported of for good works”: she raised children; she “lodged strangers”, the brothers who came to the city to visit and stayed at her house; she “washed the saints’ feet”, “relieved the afflicted”, and “diligently followed every good work.”

“But the younger widows refuse”: do not take care of them, do not provide for them. The ones under sixty, not them. “For when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry”. Wanton means lustful, sexually active, against Christ. She gave up the vow to dedicate her life to praying and fasting night and day; she got that itch and wants a man.

“Having damnation, because they have cast off their first faith.” The widowhood was nothing they took lightly. When she dedicated her life to God with prayers and fastings night and day, that was a serious thing; she could not just say, I don’t want to do this no more.
This is what the young widows will be doing: “wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.” Tattlers are gossipers.
“I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house”. Get a husband, sister, get married. “For some are already turned aside after Satan.”

“If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged”. If any believer in Christ has widows in the family, you take care of her: her son, her daughter, her uncle, her brother. Don’t burden the church, “that it may relieve them that are widows indeed”, the widows who have no family to help them. The church will take care of them.

precepts.why:
An example of a widow indeed: Anna, “a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser”. She “had lived with an husband seven years from her virginity; And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.”

She did not depart from the temple; she served God with fastings and prayers night and day. That is what widows did, and that is what it means to continue “in supplications and prayers night and day.”

sense.text: Onias told Heliodorus that some of the money belonged to Hircanus, “and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed”: that wicked Simon of the tribe of Benjamin. “The sum whereof in all was four hundred talents of silver, and two hundred of gold”.
But Heliodorus, “because of the king’s commandment”, said it must be brought into the king’s treasury, and “there was no small agony throughout the whole city.”
“But the priests, prostrating themselves before the altar in their priests’ vestments, called unto heaven”. Imagine the scene: the priests laid flat with their faces to the ground.

Whoever looked the high priest in the face saw “the inward agony of his mind”: Onias III was in agony. Why? Because he knew that their taking that money would affect a lot of our people in Jerusalem, a lot of the widows and the orphans.

“Others ran flocking out of their houses to the general supplication”; the women “girt with sackcloth”; the virgins ran to the gates, the walls and the windows; “And all, holding their hands toward heaven, made supplication.” They all started praying, and “called upon the Almighty Lord to keep the things committed of trust safe and sure”.

“The Lord of spirits, and the Prince of all power, caused a great apparition”. There appeared “an horse with a terrible rider upon him”, and “he that sat upon the horse had complete harness of gold.” That angel had a complete harness of gold.

Two other young men “scourged him continually, and gave him many sore stripes.” They were whipping the hell out of this Edomite.

Heliodorus “fell suddenly unto the ground, and was compassed with great darkness”, and was carried out, “unable to help himself with his weapons”, so that “manifestly they acknowledged the power of God.” “But they praised the Lord, that had miraculously honoured his own place”.
Heliodorus’ friends “prayed Onias”, they begged him, to call upon the most High for the life of the man “who lay ready to give up the ghost.” He was about to die.

“So the high priest, suspecting lest the king should misconceive that some treachery had been done to Heliodorus by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the health of the man.” Onias III thought it through: if the angels kill him, the angels will leave after a while, and the Greeks will come after us.
The same young men appeared and said, “Give Onias the high priest great thanks, insomuch as for his sake the Lord hath granted thee life”, and “declare unto all men the mighty power of God.”

precepts.why:
The scripture that says keeping a man’s living from him is murder: “The bread of the needy is their life: he that defraudeth him thereof is a man of blood. He that taketh away his neighbour’s living slayeth him; and he that defraudeth the labourer of his hire is a bloodshedder.”

What Simon did was no light thing. Taking the money of the widows, the orphans, the fatherless and the strangers is murder. That was their livelihood; we took care of them with that money, and he would rather have Esau come and take it all. He is a murderer.

That is why it is never just one sin. All I did was tell them about the money. No, you did worse than you think you did.

sense.text: “This Simon now, of whom we spake afore, having been a bewraye of the money, and of his country”: he revealed the secret. And he “slandered Onias, as if he had terrified Heliodorus, and been the worker of these evils.” He told the Greeks that Onias III did that to Heliodorus. This dude Simon is no damn good.

“Thus was he bold to call him a traitor, that had deserved well of the city, and tendered his own nation, and was so zealous of the laws.” He was so bold he called Onias the high priest, that type of brother, a traitor.

“But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed”: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin hated Onias III so much that one of his men killed one of Onias’s priests. That is why it is never just one thing. It is a domino effect of sins.

Onias saw “the danger of this contention, and that Apollonius, as being the governor of Celosyria and Phenice, did rage, and increase Simon’s malice”. Simon got the governor of Celosyria and Phenice to rage against Onias. Not only did he get his own group mad at Onias, he went to the other nations against the high priest. That is how far your anger will go because you can’t get your way.

“He went to the king, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private”. Onias III did not even go there to accuse Simon. It shows the character of Onias III, a great and upstanding older man.

“For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto.” Simon was causing insurrections in Jerusalem, and Onias wanted the king to look into it. Blessed are the peacemakers, and live peaceably if at all possible, but peace don’t always work with some black people.

precepts.why: “Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not.” This type of man, a partner with a thief, hates his own soul. He hears cursing and doesn’t tell it; he keeps it tucked in.

Keeping it tucked in goes against the law: “And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it; if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity.” Whatever the judgment is on that man, you get that judgment.

That is why in the hood people see murders all the time and say, I’m not saying nothing. Then weeks, a month, a year later that same person ends up dead, and people ask, what did they do, they never killed nobody? They were a witness, and they chose not to utter it.

“Or if a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil, or to do good, whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath, and it be hid from him; when he knoweth of it, then he shall be guilty in one of these.” “He shall confess that he hath sinned in that thing”.

The brothers know the story. At camp, planning who to take travelling, one brother told another to trim his unkempt hair, and he answered, well, I guess I’m not traveling then. A couple of men heard it. A young man from Detroit told it, but the officer who heard it first said he was going to tell it, he was just waiting till next week. Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me. Be mindful of brothers: they may seem decent on the outside, but be mindful of what they say or don’t say.

Simon slandered Onias III. “For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.” Slander is not a light thing.

“Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off”. Deacon Asaf has been going over classes, and there is a lot of slander in the Israelite community. They thrive off slander, off hatred, name calling, ridicule and false accusations.

God already said he will cut off people that do that, meaning he will kill them, so for you to join with these people, you’re a fool.

“Him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.” That is the high look that comes with the slander. They think God is with them, and the men and women around them, as stupid as they are, believe God is with them. God is not with them, not according to these scriptures.

“Take ye heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders. And they will deceive every one his neighbour, and will not speak the truth: they have taught their tongue to speak lies, and weary themselves to commit iniquity.”

Some people love slander; they teach their tongue to speak lies, and there are some very good liars out there. A woman caught in the midst of adultery starts crying, this is not what it looks like, and some of you men will dismiss what you saw. You just saw the plumber pull his tool out of her, and you’re such a simp: okay, babe, put your clothes on; you’re Gary the plumber, nice to meet you, my man.

A true story, back in 1998 in Boston, in another camp: a brother comes home from class and finds a dude coming out of his bedroom zipping up his pants. The brother opens the Bible and reads him the commandment against adultery, and the dude smacks the Bible out of his face. Don’t bring a man like that around us. They cannot roll with us; let them go to those other camps.

“There be three things that mine heart feareth; and for the fourth I was sore afraid: the slander of a city, the gathering together of an unruly multitude, and a false accusation: all these are worse than death.”

Simon did all of it. The slander of a city. The gathering together of an unruly multitude: he had the Greeks gather together to try to get the money from Jerusalem. And a false accusation: Onias did this. God says all these are worse than death.

Don’t tell me what they say about me; tell me why they feel comfortable telling you. In every school there is that one brother or sister all the murmurers draw to, telling him everything they don’t like about people. Why do they feel so comfortable saying evil to you? You obviously didn’t have our back.

You cannot come to the Bishop with evil. A deacon once came to him and said a sister in red shoes was a hoe, because of her high heels. The Bishop called Deacon Malachi and the others over and asked them, do you think that sister is a hoe? They said no. And he told them, well, this mother effer right here says she’s a hoe because of the shoes. He blew his spot up. You all have to learn how to do that, so that men think twice before bringing evil to you. We must train ourselves to hate evil.

Simon called Onias a traitor. “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.” Don’t bear false witness. These are basic laws, but for some reason in the black community they are so difficult.

“A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow.” Why? Because that man will get people hurt; he will get people killed. Simon’s false accusation ended in murder.
“Use not to make any manner of lie: for the custom thereof is not good.” The custom of lying is not good.

“From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.” Simon wanted the upper hand over Onias and could not get it, so what did he do? Killed. You fight and war because you ain’t praying to the Lord about it.

“Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.” When you do pray and still don’t receive, it is because you ask for the wrong reasons, with a lustful purpose that is not for the benefit of the nation.

All I did was one sin? No, there is a domino effect in your sins.

These are the attributes of Simon, and this class is a self-examination class for all of us, the Bishop included. “Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment”.

“Whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council”: Raca means thou fool, vain fellow, and the council is man’s council. “But whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.” Continue in the sin, the name calling and all of that, and it is hell fire: that is when God has to step in.

Still dealing with Simon and his hatred for Onias: “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer”. That’s Simon. “And ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”

It starts with coveting: Simon coveted power. From there it turned to anger, from anger to slander, and from slander to murder. That is the domino effect. It is never just one sin, and not only are you affected; the people you sinned against are affected.

Holding on to anger is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to die. You drink the poison waiting for somebody else to drop dead, and the only one affected is you. That goes for men and women.

That spirit Simon had, going to the other nations against his own high priest, is here: “Then certain ungodly persons, who hated their own people, went unto the king”. You will always have certain ungodly men and women among us who hate their own people.

It is the same today. When the young brother Karmelo Anthony was tried over the stabbing at the Frisco track meet, black voices online celebrated that no black people sat on the jury, called our people names, and a black woman said black supremacy is the most dangerous ideology, and that everybody, including black people, wants us gone. Where does black supremacy exist? Nobody has ever seen it. This is the same thing they did back then: a whole white jury, the white man not guilty, the black man guilty in three or four minutes. What happened to a jury of your peers? And the judge and the family had connections: a conflict of interest.

And she is not the only one who thinks like that. There are Israelites, brothers and sisters who call themselves repented, who think exactly like that; a bunch of them left in 2018. Our people forget history quick.

“Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings”. Simon was full of malice. When you give yourself to the Lord, one of the first things you must do in repenting is lay aside all malice. Guile means deceit: put it away from you. Don’t be a hypocrite. Whatever envies you’ve got, hatreds, jealousies, put them from you, and all evil speakings.

“As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby”. You cast all those sins away and start all over again, as a newborn babe. The sincere milk of the word is the commandments in Christ, and that is the only way you can grow in this truth.

Apply verses one and two and everyone will see a substantial change in your life. But if you are the same grimy brother or sister from last year and the year before that, we know you have not been applying them.
Onias III went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all”. That is a peacemaker: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.”
These are Onias’s attributes: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” That is, if it be possible.
“Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord”. Without it you cannot see the Lord. These are the attributes of Onias.

Peace don’t always work with some people. “Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified, even as it is with you”: we want the word of the Lord to have free course throughout the earth. “And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith.”

Meditate on that. Some men you can’t reason with. There is no sitting down to talk, no getting two witnesses. Some spirits are grimy: at the end of the day they don’t want peace with you, they want you dead. That was Simon; Onias saw he would not “leave his folly”.

There are Israelite camps like that. A brother at an event said shalom to a brother from one of these camps and got cursed for it. They have not faith: they teach now that Moses is in the lake of fire and that John the Baptist was a wicked Israelite. These are new blasphemous doctrines, from camps filled with hatred, and they are unreasonable.

sense.text:
“Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest”. This is Onias III’s blood brother. Not only does Onias have to deal with Simon of the tribe of Benjamin; now his own blood brother is trying to take the priesthood from him.

When problems come, they come. Put yourself in his sandals: his good friend Simon turned on him, and now his brother is trying to take the priesthood from him.

“Promising unto the king by intercession three hundred and threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue eighty talents”. That is bribery. He paid money to become the high priest, when the priesthood went by bloodline.

Sometimes it is not good enough for a brother to be the support. Onias was the high priest and his brother should have supported him, but Jason said, I can do a better job than him, and have access to all that money. You have to look at a man’s motives.

He promised more “if he might have licence to set him up a place for exercise, and for the training up of youth in the fashions of the heathen, and to write them of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians.” Not only was he bribing his way in; he convinced the king that he could get these Israelites to join the Greek games and become Hellenized. Onias wasn’t rolling like that, but his brother said, I’ll be the one to do it.
“He had gotten into his hand the rule”: Jason became high priest, and “he forthwith brought his own nation to Greekish fashion.” “He brought up new customs against the law”.
“He built gladly a place of exercise under the tower itself, and brought the chief young men under his subjection, and made them wear a hat.” That is the hat of Hermes.

“Now such was the height of Greek fashions, and increase of heathenish manners”. This is when we became Greek citizens and worshipped idols.

“That ungodly wretch, and no high priest”: although Jason got the rule, the writer says he is not the true high priest.

The priests had “no courage to serve any more at the altar, but despising the temple, and neglecting the sacrifices”, ran to the place of exercise “after the game of Discus called them forth”: the Greek games, the Olympics.

“Not setting by the honours of their fathers, but liking the glory of the Grecians best of all.” We see the same thing today. Our people love white society more than their own forefathers. Go to college and see: they love Greek society, white folks’ society, more than anything on the planet. Some of them will come against you for speaking against white folks or pointing out the injustice.

“By reason whereof sore calamity came upon them”: by reason of liking other races, the white race, better than ourselves, sore calamity came upon us. “For they had them to be their enemies and avengers”. At one time they were our enemies; now we go to them as our avengers: Mr. White Man, can you avenge me of this and that?

This chapter from verse 10 to 16 is what Paul was constantly referencing when he says there is neither Jew nor Greek. All of you men who teach on the street must know this history.

“For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God: but the time following shall declare these things.” Sometimes we take God’s laws for granted, with the mentality that I can sin and God won’t do nothing.

precepts.why:
“Seek not of the Lord preeminence, neither of the king the seat of honour.” The priesthood fell to Onias III; that was his lot. His brother said, I want it, I should have it, not my brother.

“Justify not thyself before the Lord; and boast not of thy wisdom before the king.”

All this ties into us today. “And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully.” You want to be an officer, a captain, a deacon, a bishop; you want to be moved up. You are not crowned except you strive lawfully.

What does crowned mean? “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.”

Just as Jason undermined his brother to be high priest, brothers in here have done the same. A brother kept failing the officer of fifty test and said, I’ll get a copy with the answers and pass it around. You might think that is just cheating. It is worse: the officers of fifty counsel the people. A brother who cannot pass cheats, becomes an officer of fifty, and now he is counseling marriages. He is not qualified for that rank. Captain Zakar, Deacon Isaac and others spend time making variations of the exam to see each man’s level of understanding, with many counseling questions, because the counselors must be accurate, on point and scriptural.

Who gives out the crowns? “And in the midst of them there was a young man of a high stature, taller than all the rest, and upon every one of their heads he set crowns, and was more exalted; which I marvelled at greatly.” Christ is a young man; he was crucified at thirty-three, so don’t make him look old. And taller than all the rest means by feet, not a couple of inches: you will know that is the Son of God.

“These be they that have put off the mortal clothing, and put on the immortal, and have confessed the name of God: now are they crowned, and receive palms.” “What young person is it that crowneth them, and giveth them palms in their hands?” “It is the Son of God, whom they have confessed in the world. Then began I greatly to commend them that stood so stiffly for the name of the Lord.” That crown is what we all want, and it is given to them that strive lawfully, not to the man who undermines his brother.

Jason tried to bribe his way into the high priesthood. “For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right.” That is what they were doing back there.

“All bribery and injustice shall be blotted out: but true dealing shall endure for ever.” The Most High deals with bribes. Here comes Jason, the brother of Onias the high priest, trying to bribe his way to become high priest, and the Most High will blot it out.

The “increase of heathenish manners” is why Paul wrote: “Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.” That goes back to what was just read: we became Greek and worshipped idols.

All the things Paul writes about are referenced in the histories. Paul didn’t just make stuff up; it was based on something, and it is found in the book of Maccabees. Esau conveniently took that out, so our people in Christianity are lost and confused.

It is not a light thing to do wickedly against God’s laws: “Then shall they be in pitiful case, which now have abused my ways: and they that have cast them away despitefully shall dwell in torments. For such as in their life have received benefits, and have not known me”.

Jason Whitlock said he is not oppressed because he makes ten million dollars a year. He once posted Revelation 3:9 without breaking it down, Amalek attacked him, and he quickly deleted it. Ten million a year is a benefit. A lot of our people become doctors and make big money and say, if I can do it, you can do it. They received benefits and have not known God.

“And they that have lothed my law, while they had yet liberty, and, when as yet place of repentance was open unto them, understood not, but despised it”: while they had liberty, with brothers out there teaching and the videos going on in their feed. They saw it, and they hated it.

“The same must know it after death by pain.” Who says that when you die you don’t get punished? You will know pain after death, when Christ returns. Nobody escapes.

sense.text: “This ungracious Jason”, now the high priest, sent money “to the sacrifice of Hercules”, money in honour of Hercules. Even the bearers thought it not fit to bestow it on the sacrifice.
Antiochus came to Jerusalem, “where he was honourably received of Jason, and of the city, and was brought in with torchlight, and with great shoutings”. They threw him a parade.
“Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus, the aforesaid Simon’s brother”: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin. His brother is Menelaus.
“When he had magnified him for the glorious appearance of his power”, flattering the king, he “got the priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver.”
“Bringing nothing worthy the high priesthood, but having the fury of a cruel tyrant, and the rage of a savage beast.”

“Then Jason, who had undermined his own brother, being undermined by another, was compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.” Jason undermined his own brother, and now Menelaus undermined him. What tribe was Simon? Benjamin. So what was Menelaus? Benjamin. Now the high priest is of the tribe of Benjamin. You can’t make this stuff up. Jason had to run.

“So Menelaus got the principality”: Menelaus of the tribe of Benjamin became high priest. When he was called before the king, he “left his brother Lysimachus in his stead in the priesthood”, in charge.

“Menelaus, supposing that he had gotten a convenient time, stole certain vessels of gold out of the temple”. He started stealing things out of the holy temple, “and gave some of them to Andronicus”, gave them to Esau, “and some he sold into Tyrus and the cities round about.”

“Which when Onias knew of a surety, he reproved him”: he cursed him out. Then Onias had to run for his life, and “withdrew himself into a sanctuary at Daphne, that lieth by Antiochia”, up in the north-eastern corner of the Mediterranean, to get away from the new high priest of the tribe of Benjamin.

“Menelaus, taking Andronicus apart, prayed him to get Onias into his hands”: he took him aside and whispered, I’ll pay you, get rid of this dude. Andronicus came “to Onias in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths”: I swear this, I swear that. That is what they do. Onias suspected him, “yet persuaded he him to come forth of the sanctuary: whom forthwith he shut up without regard of justice.” He killed Onias III, the real high priest.

“Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation”, because other nations respected Onias III. They complained “because Onias was slain without cause.” They knew he was killed for no reason.
“Antiochus was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead.” Even the white man was crying for Onias.

He took away Andronicus’ purple, led him through the city to the very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, “there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.”

precepts.why: “For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways.” Whatever you do is going to come back on you. However you deal in this earth with your brother and your neighbour, it comes back on you. Jason undermined his own brother, and he was undermined by another.

An easier verse: “But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons.” The world calls that karma, but the Bible says if you do wrong, you shall receive for the wrong you have done.

“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” Whatever you do in this earth, you will reap. If you decide to undermine the brother next to you, or do some deceitful stuff to your sister, it is going to come back to you. It might not be this year; it might be next year, but it is going to come.

Onias had to run. “Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to thy neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.” Sometimes brothers and sisters do something simple: wink at it. It doesn’t always have to be a counsel for small matters.

“Abstain from strife, and thou shalt diminish thy sins: for a furious man will kindle strife. A sinful man disquieteth friends, and maketh debate among them that be at peace.” “As a man’s strength is, so is his wrath”. “If thou blow the spark, it shall burn: if thou spit upon it, it shall be quenched: and both these come out of thy mouth.” Your mouth has the power: you can blow on that spark and it will burn, or spit on it and quench it. Let it go.

“Curse the whisperer and doubletongued: for such have destroyed many that were at peace. A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many, and driven them from nation to nation: strong cities hath it pulled down, and overthrown the houses of great men.” Onias had to flee from Jerusalem up into Syria. A backbiting tongue overthrew the house of a great man.

Onias had a good report among the Jews and among the other nations. He was not trying to join with the other nations; he said, I’m not joining with you, yet he still had a good report among them. “Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.”

Without means without the truth. You must have a good report outside this truth. If somebody tries to do a drive-by at camp one day because of something you did or said, what is going on? You have to have a good report within and without.

Somebody might say that is only for a man who desires the office of a bishop. No: “That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing.” You have to walk honestly toward them that are without the truth. You can’t be outside the school robbing, stealing, lying, using drugs, whatever little secret things you have going on.

Why lack of nothing? Because people out in the world will look out for you. They will say, this is a good dude, this is a good sister.
“Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.” Walk in wisdom toward them that don’t know the truth. Redeeming the time: be aware of the time you are in.

“Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.” They may speak against us as evildoers, but by our good works they will glorify God. Why? Because our people who are living like Gentiles will repent based on your conduct out there in the world.

sense.text: For almost forty days there were seen “horsemen running in the air, in cloth of gold”, troops of horsemen encountering one another, “Wherefore every man prayed that that apparition might turn to good.”

“Now when there was gone forth a false rumour”: a lie, “as though Antiochus had been dead, Jason took at the least a thousand men, and suddenly made an assault upon the city”. Jason was of the tribe of Levi. “Menelaus fled into the castle”: Menelaus of the tribe of Benjamin.

Remember 4:23-24: Jason is the one who sent Menelaus to the king, and Menelaus underhandedly took the priesthood. They were one-time friends. Now look: Menelaus is running from his friend Jason, from whom he took the priesthood.

“But Jason slew his own citizens without mercy, not considering that to get the day of them of his own nation would be a most unhappy day for him; but thinking they had been his enemies, and not his countrymen”. Why? Because he despised his own people.

“Howbeit for all this he obtained not the principality, but at the last received shame for the reward of his treason”. You think you can be a traitor and be honoured and respected? Nobody likes a traitor, not even the white man. In Rise of the Planet of the Apes, a movie about black people, the traitor apes had the word donkey painted on them. That is the brothers who were here in 2018, and some of the brothers who just bugged out in LA: donkey. You cannot be trusted.

“In the end therefore he had an unhappy return, being accused before Aretas the king of the Arabians, fleeing from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the laws, and being had in abomination as an open enemy of his country and countrymen”. See all that evil he did with Onias; it all came back on him.

“Thus he that had driven many out of their country perished in a strange land”. He did that to a lot of Israelites, and now it happened to him. He retired “to the Lacedemonians, and thinking there to find succour by reason of his kindred”: Lacedemonia is Sparta, in southern Greece, where his kindred were.
“And he that had cast out many unburied had none to mourn for him”. Nobody cried for him. Imagine a burial where nobody gives a damn; they spit on your grave.

When word came to the king, “he thought that Judea had revolted”. Because of all the commotion this dude caused, this Edomite king took the city by force of arms. “There were destroyed within the space of three whole days fourscore thousand”, eighty thousand, “whereof forty thousand were slain in the conflict; and no fewer sold than slain.” They sold some into slavery.

He went into the most holy temple, “Menelaus, that traitor to the laws, and to his own country, being his guide”. He guided Esau on what to do, and remember, this is an Israelite. Antiochus took “the holy vessels with polluted hands” and gave away the things dedicated to the place.

“The Lord was angry for a while for the sins of them that dwelt in the city, and therefore his eye was not upon the place.” His eye was not on the place means God was not protecting us, because when Onias left, sins came back into the city.

“For had they not been formerly wrapped in many sins, this man, as soon as he had come, had forthwith been scourged, and put back from his presumption, as Heliodorus was”. When Onias was there the laws were kept very well; as soon as he left, all hell broke loose with that damn Jason and Menelaus.

“Nevertheless God did not choose the people for the place’s sake”: he chose the place for the people. The people are more important. And as the place “was forsaken in the wrath of the Almighty, so again, the great Lord being reconciled, it was set up with all glory.”

Antiochus carried out “a thousand and eight hundred talents” and “left governors to vex the nation”, and besides them “Menelaus, who worse than all the rest bare an heavy hand over the citizens, having a malicious mind against his countrymen the Jews.” The Israelite was worse than Esau, heavy handed over his own people. You can’t make this stuff up.

That is why today they look for those good black negroes: they know they will be harder on us than Esau, because they have something to prove. They look for negroes who will be harsh and critical on other black people and never have any remorse for their own race.

“That detestable ringleader Apollonius” came with twenty-two thousand men, commanded “to slay all those that were in their best age, and to sell the women and the younger sort”: selling the women and the young ones into slavery.
“Pretending peace, did forbear till the holy day of the sabbath”, and then “he slew all them that were gone to the celebrating of the sabbath”.

“But Judas Maccabeus with nine others, or thereabout, withdrew himself into the wilderness, and lived in the mountains after the manner of beasts, with his company, who fed on herbs continually, lest they should be partakers of the pollution.”

precepts.why: Christ’s word on the man who betrays: “it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.” This is spoken of him that shall “offend one of these little ones which believe in me”.

The verse about betraying Christ himself: “The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born.”

Two verses, and both mean the same for a traitor: go die. That is the reward of treason Jason received.

God did not choose the people for the place’s sake. It is the same thing Christ said: “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath”. He is talking about the Israelites. Why? Because the people are more important.

sense.text: What happened to Menelaus, who was wicked as hell, is not found until chapter 13. He “joined himself with them, and with great dissimulation encouraged Antiochus, not for the safeguard of the country, but because he thought to have been made governor.” If I can’t be high priest again, I’ll be governor.

“But the King of kings moved Antiochus’ mind against this wicked wretch”. The Lord moved Antiochus’s mind: one day you’re friends, and the Most High says, snap, that’s not your friend, I want you to hate him. “And Lysias informed the king that this man was the cause of all mischief”. It is all coming out now.

At Berea was “a tower of fifty cubits high, full of ashes”, where whoever “was condemned of sacrilege, or had committed any other grievous crime” was thrust in to his death. “Such a death it happened that wicked man to die, not having so much as burial in the earth; and that most justly: For inasmuch as he had committed many sins about the altar, whose fire and ashes were holy, he received his death in ashes.” He got his just reward.

“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?” Today’s class is about self-examination, for all of us.

One brother just left because, he said, Captain Abiel was putting too much pressure on him: he was forcing him to go out and teach, to do God’s work, to be accountable. Spirits like that, just leave. Nobody is going to cry over spilled milk.

precepts.why: “Before judgment examine thyself, and in the day of visitation thou shalt find mercy.” Examine yourselves: it goes for all of us.

sense.text: When the Pharisees heard Christ had put the Sadducees to silence, a lawyer asked him, tempting him, “Master, which is the great commandment in the law?”

“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment.” Of the ten commandments, the first four deal with this one: have no other gods, make no graven image, take not the name of the Lord in vain, remember the sabbath day to keep it holy. There are many more commandments, but this deals with the ten.

“And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” The next six deal with loving your neighbour as yourself: honour thy father and mother, do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not covet.

Thou shalt not covet is number ten, but that is where all the others above it start, in your mind, because coveting is an internal thing within you and me.

“On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” What was read in Maccabees today pertains to those two great commandments.

Nothing read today had anything to do with a big butt woman. There was no lust for sex in anything read; that wasn’t these men’s problem. Their problem was covetousness: wanting to be the top dog, power. Some men covet power and authority. Everybody ain’t coveting the big bad black woman’s butt. Sorry, brothers: everybody ain’t got your demon.

Write these down: covetousness for power and authority, hatred, betrayal, a traitor, lies, theft, stealing from the temple, and murder. That is what was read in today’s lesson, and it all occurred because of covetousness: men wanting certain seats of authority. Christians never discuss or examine themselves when it comes to these sins.
